strengths: Well-motivated problem: Figure 2 clearly demonstrates that detection performance is suppressed when track queries are present in MOTR, establishing a clear empirical motivation for decoupling.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Thorough experiments across multiple datasets (DanceTrack, BFT, AnimalTrack, MOT17) with detailed ablations (Tables 1, 4-7) and careful component analysis.

Novel diagnostic framework: Track Attention Mass provides a principled, cardinality-corrected lens for analyzing attention imbalance in joint decoders, with insights about dataset-specific attention calibration (Appendix B).

Strong performance on specialized benchmarks: Achieves leading HOTA (71.1) on BFT and best end-to-end results on AnimalTrack, demonstrating effectiveness in dynamic scenarios with severe deformations.
Practical efficiency analysis: Shows detection pass saturates at shallow depths (Figure 6), enabling compact dual-pass design at 20.7 FPS with modest overhead—valuable for practitioners.
Rigorous ablation studies: Cumulative ablations (Table 6) and sensitivity analyses clearly decompose contributions and validate design choices.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and overclaimed 'detector-free' contribution: The core idea—running detection inference before tracking—is straightforward. Table 1 shows minimal gains over frozen external detectors (58.0→58.2 HOTA, Δ0.2). The internal vs. external distinction is artificial since both require detection inference. The term 'detector-free' is misleading.

Marginal and inconsistent improvements on primary benchmark: SelfMOTR (69.2 HOTA) slightly underperforms CO-MOT (69.4 HOTA) on DanceTrack. DetA is lower (80.9 vs. 82.1) despite claims of better detection. Main advantage (AssA 59.3 vs. 58.9) lacks rigorous justification beyond 'feature alignment'.

Poor generalization to realistic benchmarks: MOT17 results show substantial underperformance (57.5–58.4 HOTA vs. CO-MOT's 60.1 HOTA, ~2.6 point gap). Paper acknowledges this but doesn't explain why decoupling fails in crowded real-world scenarios, limiting practical impact.

Track Attention Mass analysis lacks causal justification: While Figure 5 shows more balanced entropy, the paper doesn't prove this *causes* performance gains. Alternative explanations exist: additional supervision signals, architectural changes, or implicit regularization from dual passes. The analysis is correlative, not mechanistic.

Confounded experimental setup undermines fair comparison: Incorporates QIMv2 and query denoising (MOTRv2/v3 components), joint CrowdHuman training (Δ4.3 HOTA in Table 4b). Unclear if CO-MOT and other baselines use these. Cumulative ablation (Table 6) shows most gains come from HSV augmentation and CrowdHuman (Δ5.1), not self-proposals.

Unjustified design choices: Why confidence-modulated content (PE(confidence)) for proposals? Why exactly 10 learned anchors? Why λ_prop=0.5? No ablations on these hyperparameters; choices appear ad-hoc.

Incomplete efficiency comparison: No end-to-end latency comparison between two-pass vs. single-pass. FPS comparison to recent methods (CO-MOT, MOTRv3) missing. Memory and infrastructure overhead not discussed.

Limited scope and narrow generalization: Only human tracking (DanceTrack) and animals (BFT, AnimalTrack). No vehicles or diverse object categories tested. MOT17 failure suggests method is dataset-specific, raising generalization concerns.
Missing analysis of failure modes and case studies: No qualitative examples of where/why SelfMOTR succeeds or fails. No investigation of cases where decoupling hurts performance. No error analysis.
Lack of statistical rigor: No confidence intervals or significance testing. Improvements on DanceTrack (0.2–0.4 HOTA) often within noise margins. Claims of superiority should acknowledge uncertainty.

Superficial connection to LLM attention sinks: Parallel to attention sink literature (Gu et al. 2025) is borrowed but not deeply explored. Differences between transformer tracking and language model dynamics not discussed.

Incremental contribution: No novel detection or association algorithms. Primarily a reorganization of existing MOTR components. Contribution feels more engineering-oriented than research-advancing for a top venue.
